title: Global growth remains solid in a challenging environment
gist: PIIE's Fall 2026 outlook sees solid global growth (3.2% in 2026, 3.1% in 2027) cushioned by the AI boom against Iran-war energy prices, with the Fed hiking and US fiscal risks rising.

insights.claim: PIIE projects real global GDP growth of 3.2% in 2026 and 3.1% in 2027, with US growth of 2.3% in 2026 and 2.2% in 2027.
insights.speaker: Karen Dynan
insights.so_what: Baseline is growth with higher rates rather than recession.

insights.claim: The Iran war lifted Brent to about $100 a barrel, roughly 40% above its pre-war level, and the forecast assumes Brent drifts to just over $80 by end-2027 in line with futures.
insights.speaker: Karen Dynan
insights.so_what: Outlook depends on energy prices retreating on schedule.

insights.claim: Higher interest rates will be an important force holding back growth next year, and government borrowing rates in many advanced economies are at their highest since the global financial crisis due partly to fiscal worries and AI-buildout competition for loanable funds.
insights.speaker: Karen Dynan
insights.so_what: AI capex competes with governments for capital, pressuring long yields.

insights.claim: Chinese domestic demand stays weak from overcapacity and the property slump, and the strength of Chinese exports is likely to fade next year, while India leads emerging markets.
insights.speaker: Karen Dynan
insights.so_what: China export fade and India strength are relative-value themes.
insights.locator: Growth in most of the major economies

insights.claim: The FOMC raised the policy rate by 25bp in September and the most likely path is three more quarter-point hikes in December, January and March.
insights.speaker: Karen Dynan
insights.so_what: Positioning for further Fed tightening through Q1 2027.

insights.claim: PCE inflation is projected at 3.7% over 2026, easing to 2.3% in 2027, while core PCE is 3.3% in 2026 and 2.7% in 2027.
insights.speaker: Karen Dynan
insights.so_what: Core falls more slowly than headline due to services inflation, diesel pass-through and chip shortages.

insights.claim: US consumer spending is mainly propped up by household wealth gains from AI optimism in equities, so a significant equity correction could sharply weaken spending.
insights.speaker: Karen Dynan
insights.so_what: Equity-market wealth effect is the key downside risk to growth.

insights.claim: US AI equipment spending is surging, but much of the equipment is imported, limiting its immediate GDP contribution.
insights.speaker: Karen Dynan
insights.so_what: AI capex boosts imports (Asia chip exporters) more than near-term US GDP.

insights.claim: Net federal interest payments relative to GDP are at their highest since the 1990s, and the 10-year yield is about a percentage point above the CBO's early-2026 projection.
insights.speaker: Karen Dynan

insights.claim: Treasury ownership has shifted from foreign official holders to leveraged hedge funds and households, so a rate shock could be amplified by hedge fund deleveraging.
insights.speaker: Karen Dynan
insights.so_what: Basis-trade deleveraging is a Treasury-market tail risk.

insights.claim: AI will probably improve the fiscal outlook but will not solve it, since faster productivity also tends to raise interest rates and income shifting to capital lowers average tax rates.
insights.speaker: Karen Dynan
insights.so_what: Don't count on AI productivity to close deficits.
insights.quote: AI will probably improve the fiscal outlook, but it will not solve the problem.

insights.claim: A US fiscal crisis does not appear imminent, but the risk has grown and political polarization argues against meaningful near-term action.
insights.speaker: Karen Dynan
insights.so_what: Slow-burn risk rather than a near-term trigger.
